pages.x: The Seljuks were a clan of Oghuz Turks, herders and horse archers from the steppe east of the Caspian Sea, who had become Muslims. Led by two brothers, Tughril and Chaghri, they moved into Khorasan, and in 1040 at Dandanaqan they routed the army of the Ghaznavid sultan and its war elephants.

Tughril took Persia city by city, and in 1055 he entered Baghdad, home of the caliph, the spiritual head of Sunni Muslims, who had long been under the thumb of the Shia Buyid dynasty. The caliph named him sultan, and the Turks became the sword of Sunni Islam.

In 1071 Tughril's nephew, Alp Arslan, met the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert, in eastern Anatolia. Part of the Byzantine army deserted or held back, and the Turks' horse archers surrounded the rest. Romanos was captured, the first Byzantine emperor ever taken prisoner by a Muslim ruler.

Romanos was brought before Alp Arslan, who asked him what he would have done if their places were reversed. Perhaps killed you, or paraded you through the streets of Constantinople, said Romanos. My punishment is far heavier, the sultan replied: I forgive you, and set you free.

Romanos was overthrown and blinded by his rivals at home, and Byzantium fell into civil war. Turkish bands poured into Anatolia, and within a few years they had reached the Aegean. A branch of the Seljuks founded the Sultanate of Rum there, Rum meaning Rome, with its capital at Nicaea and later Konya.

Under Malik Shah, sultan from 1072 to 1092, the empire stretched from Central Asia to the Mediterranean, run by a brilliant Persian minister, Nizam al-Mulk, who founded colleges across it. In 1095 the Byzantine emperor asked the pope for help against the Turks, and the answer was the First Crusade.

The Seljuks brought the Turks into the heart of the Islamic world, where Turkish soldiers and dynasties would rule for centuries. They made Anatolia Turkish, set off the Crusades, and left mosques and caravanserais that still stand.
